edits.to: يدة في كونها مفيدة للعمل، ⟨ومنها جزئية وقريبة في كونها مفيدة للعمل⟩. فالجزئية كالعلم بأحكام
edits.old: إن المعارف والعلوم ثلاثة أصناف: إما معرفة غايتها الاعتقاد الحاصل عنها في النفس فقط، كالعلم بحدث العالم، والقول بالجزء الذي لا يتجزأ وأشباه ذلك. وإما معرفة غايتها العمل، وهذه منها كلية وبعيدة في كونها مفيدة للعمل. فالجزئية كالعلم بأحكام الصلاة والزكاة وما أشبههما من جزئيات الفرائض والسنن. والكلية كالعلم بالأصول التي تبنى عليها هذه الفروع من الكتاب والسنة والإجماع، والعلم بالأحكام الحاصلة عن هذه الأصول على الإطلاق وأقسامها، وما يلحقها من حيث هي أحكام.

edits.old: Forms of knowledge and the sciences are of three kinds. There is knowledge whose end is simply the belief it produces in the soul: for example, knowledge that the world has come into being, the doctrine of the indivisible part, and similar matters. There is knowledge whose end is action. Some of this is universal (كلية), and remote in the assistance it affords to action. Particular knowledge (الجزئية) includes knowledge of the rulings governing prayer and almsgiving, and similar particular obligatory and customary observances. Universal knowledge includes knowledge of the principles on which these branches are built—the Book, the Sunna, and consensus—and knowledge of the rulings derived from these principles in general, their divisions, and what attaches to them insofar as they are rulings (أحكام).

edits.old: The Muʿtazilites held that goodness and badness are intrinsic attributes of acts. Some are apprehended through rational necessity, as with lying and thanking a benefactor; others, with the Law's assistance, as with ritual purification and prayer, because of, for example, the utterance that restrains indecency and the cleanliness they involve. The benefit of knowing this disagreement within this craft becomes apparent when investigating analogy from a suitable, plausible ground (القياس المناسب والمخيل), with all its kinds, and when investigating whether those exercising independent judgement are correct or mistaken.

edits.to: dness have no existence as intrinsic properties of things in external reality.
edits.old: The argument of the People of the Sunna is that ‘good’ and ‘bad’ have several meanings in the usage of speakers. The first and most familiar is what accords with or opposes the purpose of the person judging it good: one person, for instance, may find a dark complexion good and another find it bad. This is a relational matter, unlike the blackness and whiteness belonging to things in themselves. The second is what the Law has declared good or bad. The third meaning of ‘good’ is what a person is permitted to do. All these are relational, not intrinsic, attributes. This means that goodness and badness have no existence ‘outside the concrete entity.’

edits.old: They have disagreed about a morally transgressive person who acts on an interpretation (الفاسق المتأول), meaning someone who does not recognise his own transgression. Whoever holds that transgression prevents acceptance only because it arouses suspicion cannot conceive rejecting him unless his transgression consists in permitting lying. Whoever holds that transgression itself defeats acceptance, because of suspicion, permits their testimony concerning one another. The first is al-Shāfiʿī's doctrine; the second, the Qāḍī's. Al-Shāfiʿī's doctrine seems more consistent with the reasoning, and is supported by the Companions' acceptance—may God be pleased with them—of reports from the Khārijites.

edits.old: Question. edits.to: ضاء) does not require a renewed command. Those who care
edits.old: Question. The jurists’ position is that an obligation to make up a missed observance (قضاء) does not require a [renewed] command. Those who carefully distinguish the issues hold that a command to worship at a specified time does not require making it up. Specifying a time for worship—prayer at midday or fasting in Ramadan—is like specifying a place for pilgrimage or a direction for prayer. If the commanded condition is absent, the command ceases to apply, when it was on account of that condition that the command concerning the act was issued.

edits.from: ا أن يلتحق بالمرتبة الثالثة وهي التي في معنى الأصل
edits.to: ا أن يلتحق بالمرتبة الثانية وهي التي في معنى الأصل
edits.old: ويشبه أن يكون جل ما يقع في هذا الجنس مجملا، إلا أن يلتحق بالمرتبة الثالثة وهي التي في معنى الأصل. ومثل هذا قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «لا تبيعوا البر بالبر الأربعة المعلومة إلا هاء بهاء»، فإن قوما قالوا أراد بذلك المقتات، وقوما قالوا المطعوم، وقوما قالوا المكيل. وهذا كله ظن منهم، فإن الاقتيات أو الكيل أو الطعم صفة حاصرة للأمر المناسب الموجب للتحريم، وهي بالجملة فيما يظهر لي أبعد قرينة يصار إليها إلى أن يفهم عن اللفظ الجزئي المعنى الكلي، ولهذا كثير من الناس اقتصر بمثل هذا الحديث على مقتضى اللفظ.

edits.old: وَيُشْبِهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ جُلُّ مَا يَقَعُ فِي هَذَا الْجِنْسِ مُجْمَلًا، إِلَّا أَنْ يَلْتَحِقَ بِالْمَرْتَبَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ وَهِيَ الَّتِي فِي مَعْنَى الْأَصْلِ. وَمِثْلُ هَذَا قَوْلُهُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: «لَا تَبِيعُوا الْبُرَّ بِالْبُرِّ الْأَرْبَعَةَ الْمَعْلُومَةَ إِلَّا هَاءَ بِهَاءَ»، فَإِنَّ قَوْمًا قَالُوا أَرَادَ بِذَلِكَ الْمُقْتَاتَ، وَقَوْمًا قَالُوا الْمَطْعُومَ، وَقَوْمًا قَالُوا الْمَكِيلَ. وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ ظَنٌّ مِنْهُمْ، فَإِنَّ الِاقْتِيَاتَ أَوِ الْكَيْلَ أَوِ الطَّعْمَ صِفَةٌ حَاصِرَةٌ لِلْأَمْرِ الْمُنَاسِبِ الْمُوجِبِ لِلتَّحْرِيمِ، وَهِيَ بِالْجُمْلَةِ فِيمَا يَظْهَرُ لِي أَبْعَدُ قَرِينَةٍ يُصَارُ إِلَيْهَا إِلَى أَنْ يُفْهَمَ عَنِ اللَّفْظِ الْجُزْئِيِّ الْمَعْنَى الْكُلِّيُّ، وَلِهَذَا كَثِيرٌ مِنَ النَّاسِ اقْتَصَرَ بِمِثْلِ هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ عَلَى مُقْتَضَى اللَّفْظِ.

edits.to: e, unless they join the second rank, which is within
edits.old: Most cases of this kind seem indeterminate, unless they join the third rank, which is within the meaning of the original case. An example is his saying, God bless him and grant him peace, “Do not sell wheat for wheat—the four known commodities—except hand to hand.” Some say he intended staple nourishment, some food, and some goods measured by volume. All this is their probable judgement: nourishment, measure, or edibility circumscribes the suitable factor requiring prohibition. To me this seems the remotest contextual indication used to understand a universal meaning from a particular expression. Many therefore confine such a report to what its wording requires.

edits.to: extual indications that make expressions prima facie
edits.old: The Ẓāhirīs, and anyone allowing inference from expressions’ prima facie forms, should therefore not deny analogy within the original case’s meaning, or analogy from a plausible and congruently suitable ground, when the Law demonstrably attends to its proximate kind. These are all contextual indications that [make] expressions prima facie through their understood meanings, even when they are not so through their forms. There is no sense in recognising prima facie signification only in verbal form.

notes.text: Textual and doctrinal crux (scholarly review, 5 November 2026): Both al-ʿAlawī (1994, p. 44) and Bou Akl (2015, Arabic p. 130, French p. 131, §23) print “لا يتصور دون الضرر أو النفع”. Neither the negation “لا” nor the disjunction “أو النفع” should be removed without manuscript or stronger internal evidence. In al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā (discussion of the definition of the obligatory), obligation is intelligible through the preference of performance to omission in relation to human interests (أغراضنا). This is not a claim that moral obligation derives from intrinsic, rationally measurable utility. Yet Ibn Rushd’s stated reason for including a threat of punishment remains compressed: benefit also accompanies recommended acts, while threatened harm for omission helps distinguish obligation. The possible logical tension should be flagged, not silently emended.

Scope correction following scholarly review, 5 November 2026: “من هذا” concerns the entire class of obligations not specified by a fixed measure, including both wiping the head (مسح الرأس) and stillness in bowing (الطمأنينة في الركوع); the earlier phrase “In the latter case” misleadingly restricted the rule to the second example. Compare al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā, on the minimum that meets the name, with particular clarity for acts performed in sequence. His discussion also distinguishes simultaneous from successive performance; Ibn Rushd formulates the restriction more briefly.

Editorial correction to the basmala analogy (§64, al-ʿAlawī 1994 p. 69): the printed Arabic reads “مما لم يصرح بكونه من غير القرآن”, yielding a self-defeating negative. Bou Akl (2015), commentary on §81, pp. 373–374, expressly proposes emending lam yuṣarraḥa to qad ṣurriḥa, supported by al-Ghazālī’s al-Mustaṣfā and by the contrast with the basmala. The edited Arabic now shows ⟨قد صرح⟩ in angle brackets, while the 1994 reading is recorded here. This is an editorial emendation, not claimed as independently witnessed manuscript text; English already reflects it.

Source correction (5 Nov 2026): al-ʿAlawī 1994, p. 34, omits the corresponding second member after “وهذه منها كلية وبعيدة في كونها مفيدة للعمل”. Ziad Bou Akl’s 2015 Arabic edition, §2, Arabic p. 118 (PDF p. 128), includes the Escorial-witnessed “ومنها جزئية وقريبة في كونها مفيدة للعمل” (marked [أ] in his apparatus). The revised bilingual reading text supplies this clause in angle brackets; it is a reported witness reading, not an independently collated manuscript. The source omitted clause remains identifiable here.

سِبَار denotes a device or method for testing and examining. The older English “probe” captured a concrete lexical image but misleadingly foregrounded a physical instrument; “instrument of investigation” better conveys Ibn Rushd’s application to thought, together with قَانُون (“rule”). The compass and straightedge are analogies for disciplined inference, not an identification with laboratory probing. Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab, s.v. سبر. Revision after scholarly feedback, 5 November 2026.

“This book” refers to al-Ghazālī’s al-Mustaṣfā (1994 p. 37). The expression المتكلمين is rendered “mutakallimūn (practitioners of kalām)” rather than generic “speakers” or simply “those discussing this craft”, in accordance with Shaykh Ruzwan’s linguistic guidance supplied in the project. The qualification “within this discipline” identifies their work in legal theory, not the attribution of a theological position to every jurist.

The reading اللفظ المانع من الفحشاء in §11 is retained from al-ʿAlawī p. 41, although the relationship of the “utterance” to prayer and purification is not securely established; one should not silently substitute an unattested phrase. Separately خارج العين has been translated as denying intrinsic moral properties of the externally existing act, not denying every extramental relational reality. Bou Akl (2015), commentary on the corresponding argument, p. 341, analyses the relation between moral qualification and standpoint.

Correction following external scholarly review, 5 November 2026: The former editorial supplement “[is the error of supposing]” reversed the argument and has been withdrawn. “وأبين من هذا” introduces a more evident reversion to the earlier permissibility, not a second mistake. See Bou Akl (2015), French §34, p. 137 and commentary p. 354, as well as al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā, on abrogation of obligation. The inferential move assumes the absence of an independently operative demand or a new legislative ruling; negating obligation alone does not logically entail permission.

The 1994 printed Arabic of §29 (p. 49) is grammatically defective beginning فإن من يدل عنده لفظة, and this source has not here been independently re-collated with the Escorial manuscript. Bou Akl 2015, §38, French p. 139 (PDF p. 149), offers a reconstructed reading of the argument: a prohibition narrowed by a quality after an unconditional obligation may be read as disapproval; an external qualification is even stronger. The English reports this sense in square brackets, not as an unqualified translation of the broken sentence. No unverified Arabic words have been introduced into the base.

Arabic al-ʿAlawī reads “مجهولا عند الله” (“unknown to God”). The subject is the Prophet’s acceptance of the Bedouin’s crescent testimony; the argument requires the opponent to dispute that the Prophet lacked knowledge of the Bedouin’s probity. Bou Akl 2015 French §113, p. 189, explicitly has “inconnu pour le Prophète”. English adopts that referent, while the defective Arabic is retained and expressly reported; an exact manuscript-based Arabic substitution is not asserted.

The 1994 text lacks “لا” before “لموضع التهمة” in this contrast. The first position excludes reports because of suspicion; the second treats the state of transgression as itself disqualifying, irrespective of suspicion. Bou Akl (2015), §115, French p. 189, translates with supplied “⟨et non⟩ en raison de l’accusation”. The revised Arabic supplies ⟨لا⟩ as a conjectural clarification, with this note preserving the printed wording “هادم للقبول لموضع التهمة”. The following exceptional permission regarding testimony remains difficult; it is not a general rule of admissibility.

Two distinct source interventions at §97: (1) Bou Akl 2015, Arabic §119, p. 190 (PDF p. 200), reports manuscript [أ] “بالقول” against al-ʿAlawī [ع] “بالقبول”; this edition adopts the manuscript-witnessed “by statement”. (2) On Arabic p. 192 (PDF p. 202), Bou Akl emends the defective shared reading “التجرح” to “التصريح”, drawing on al-Ghazālī’s al-Mustaṣfā (see his note 23, French p. 193). The revised Arabic uses angle brackets for this *conjecture*, and English follows its carefully qualified meaning. The first correction is witness-supported; the second is an editorial emendation.

The printed phrase excludes the feminine/singulative ending (هاء التأنيث) and nevertheless lists “الثمرة والنخلة والمرأة”, all containing the feminine ending. It cannot be treated as a consistent set of examples of suffix-free generic terms. Bou Akl 2015 French §205 p. 257 and commentary p. 435–436 explains that -at can function as a singulative marker in collective nouns; absence of this ending supports genuinely collective generic force. The English retains the printed examples with this critical qualification. No unsupported emendation is inserted into Arabic; readers should distinguish the grammatical rule from these problematic examples.

The printed citation “ولا تقل لهما أف” is not the exact Qurʾānic opening of Q 17:23, which has “فلا تقل لهما أف”. The reader retains Ibn Rushd’s cited wording as transmitted, but the Qurʾānic reference must be checked against the original Qurʾān when used as a textual proof. This is not a semantic difference sufficient to reverse his a fortiori reasoning.

Three interventions in §203 against the 1994 print: (1) al-ʿAlawī has الاقتصار, where Bou Akl 2015, Arabic §250, p. 284 (PDF p. 294), reports [أ] الاقتضاء, adopted as “demand”; (2) both printings duplicate الندب in “إما على جهة الندب وإما على جهة الندب”, while Bou Akl conjectures الوجوب as the first member; it is marked ⟨الوجوب⟩; (3) in the second passage [أ] offers “إيجابا” against [ع] “إباحة”, so the sentence can concede obligation or recommendation even though removal of restriction is the predominant reading. The 1994 forms remain documented here, not silently replaced.

Critical-edition reading established: Bou Akl 2015 Arabic §251, p. 284 (PDF p. 294) reports Escorial [أ] “مجدد” (renewed) against al-ʿAlawī [ع] “محدد” (specified). The revised Arabic adopts the witnessed “renewed”; English reflects the reported manuscript reading. This is not merely a semantic conjecture.

The first two problematic expressions in §205 have reliable source control. Bou Akl 2015 Arabic §252, p. 284 (PDF p. 294), reports manuscript [أ] “الإجزاء” and “لا يقتضي الإجزاء” against [ع] “الجزاء” and “لا يقتضي إلا جزاء”. The reader now adopts the reported witness readings; the English accordingly states that compliance discharges an obligation when the command is fully fulfilled. The 1994 printed readings are documented here.

The 1994 print has “المرتبة الثالثة”; Bou Akl 2015, Arabic §267, p. 294 (PDF p. 304), records manuscript [أ] “المرتبة الثانية” against [ع] “الثالثة”. The revised text follows this witness, which also agrees with the definition of “في معنى الأصل” in §§216–217. The original reading is preserved here in the apparatus. The compressed “wheat for wheat / four commodities” quotation remains elliptical.

The transmitted reading in al-ʿAlawī 1994 §224 is “قرائن نظير الألفاظ ظاهرة”, syntactically defective. Bou Akl 2015, Arabic §273, p. 298 (PDF p. 308), emends the shared manuscript and printed reading “نظير” to “تصير” (his apparatus reports “نظير [أ][ع]”). The revised Arabic brackets ⟨تصير⟩ expressly as an editorial *conjecture*, and English translates the resulting clause. The original reading is preserved here; there is no claim that the manuscript transmits the corrected verb.

The reading ⟨تُصَيِّرُ⟩ is editorial, following Bou Akl §273, not a word independently verified in an earlier manuscript. Its grammatical government of الألفاظَ and ظاهرةً restores the clause’s logical force: contextual indications can make wording apparently significant through its understood sense, not merely its form.

The 1994 print jumps directly from “بقرينة حال أو لفظ” to “كالمتوسط بين هذين”, omitting the conclusion of the second class and the introduction of the third. Bou Akl 2015, Arabic §278, p. 302 (PDF p. 312), supplies ⟨أنه مختص. والثالث هو⟩ to restore the classification. This reading edition follows the editorial supplement, adding the appropriate pronoun “به” for readable syntax, in visible angle brackets. The 1994 lacuna is noted; no manuscript recovery is claimed. English explicitly matches the supplemental status.
